reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Wyatt had three little seeds. He wanted to grow carrots. He put one seed on top of the dirt. He pushed the other seeds down into the dirt. Then he gave them water from a spoon.

Every day Wyatt looked at his garden. "Will my seeds wake up?" he asked. Soon two little green leaves popped up. Then two more. But the spot with the seed on top stayed bare. "Why is that spot empty?" Wyatt wondered.

A bird hopped down. The bird began to chew the seed lying on top. Chew, chew, gone! Wyatt's mouth fell open. "The bird ate it!" he said. "The dirt hid my other seeds. That is why they are safe."

The leaves grew tall and straight. They grew and grew. At last, Wyatt pulled one up. A fat orange carrot hung from the leaves! He washed it with the hose. He took a big bite. "My carrot grew because the dirt kept it," he said. "And I gave it water every day too." He ran to show his mom, carrot held high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Amira ran to the window at school. She saw dark clouds. Then she heard a big boom. The boom was loud. The loud boom made Amira feel scared. Her tummy felt tight.

Her friend Ben fell down by the blocks. He cried big tears. Falling down made Ben feel sad. Amira patted his back. "It is okay," she said.

Then Miss Kim held up a red kite. "We will fly it outside after the rain," she said. Amira jumped up and down. The kite made her feel excited. Her heart went fast, like a drum.

Outside, the sun came back. Amira flew the red kite high. A bird flew by with twigs in its beak. It was making a nest in the big tree. "The bird is happy too," said Amira. Ben smiled and held her hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She ran to the block corner. So many blocks! She grabbed a circle block first. She stacked it on a square block. Roll! The circle block wobbled and rolled away. "Oh no!" said Lillian. The silly snake had no floor now.

Lillian picked up the circle block again. She pushed it on the rug. It rolled far, far away. Then she pushed a square block. It did not roll. It sat still. "The circle rolls because it is round!" said Lillian. "The square has flat sides. It stays!"

She stacked square blocks for the floor. She added rectangle blocks for the walls. She put triangle blocks on top, like a roof. The house stood tall. Lillian put the snake inside. Then she grabbed orange crayons to color a door. "Knock knock!" she said. "Who is there? A snake in a square house!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Owen steps into the waiting room. He holds Mama's hand. There are chairs and a fish tank. One fish is orange. Owen waits and watches the fish swim.

A nurse calls his name. Owen needs a shot today. He wants to be big and brave. He steps into the little room and sits on Mama's lap. The nurse cleans his arm with a cold wet wipe. Owen shivers. "Why is it cold?" he asks. "To make my arm super clean," he says to himself.

Then Mama gives him a big hug. Her arms squeeze his arm tight. The nurse counts, "One, two, three." The quick pinch comes. But it feels small, so small! Owen looks down. It is all done. "The hug squeezed my arm," Owen says. "So the pinch felt little!" The nurse puts a nice round bandage on his arm. Owen steps out and waves to the orange fish. "Goodbye, fish," he says.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Lena wanted new stickers. Yesterday, Mom had said, "Tomorrow we go to the store." Lena woke up early. Was it tomorrow now? She looked out the window. The sun was up. A loud bird sang by her bed.

"Mom, is it tomorrow?" Lena asked. Mom smiled. "Yesterday we said tomorrow. Now it is today. Today is the day we go." Lena clapped her hands. Sleep had turned tomorrow into today! "So tonight I sleep again?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "And later, tomorrow comes back."

Lena picked her shoes. She put them on now, not later. At the store she found star stickers. She held them tight. "Thank you, today," Lena whispered. At bedtime she looked at her stickers. Tonight was for sleeping. Tomorrow was for more. "Goodnight, tomorrow," she said. She turned off the light.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Athena wanted to play at the park. But the sky looked gray. Dark clouds sat over the swings.

"Mama, is it going to rain?" she asked.

"Maybe," said Mama. "Feel the wind. It is windy today."

The wind blew hard. It took Athena's hat right off. The hat flew over the brown grass. Athena ran and caught it. "The wind pushed my hat," she said. "Because it is windy."

Mama opened her bag. She pulled out rain boots. "Put these on. If it rains, your shoes stay dry." Athena pushed her feet into the boots. Then the rain came. Drip, drip, drip. Athena looked down. Her boots were dry! "My feet are dry," she said. "Because I have my boots."

Mama held out a warm coat. Athena zipped it up. The rain made little sounds on her hood. Tappity tap. It sounded like tiny drums.

When the rain stopped, the sun came out. "Look, it is sunny now," said Athena. The sun helped a puddle grow smaller and smaller. Athena stomped in it with her boots. Splash! Her feet were still dry. "Sunny days and rainy days are both fun," said Athena.

Mama laughed. "Yes. And hot cocoa waits at home." They walked home together, hand in hand, boots still warm and dry.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. She wanted to count them all by herself.

"One, two, three," she said. She tapped a pea each time. Then she stopped. What came next? She peeked at her big brother, Ben. "I forgot the next one," she said. She looked upset.

"You can start at one again," said Ben. "Songs go back to the start." Aubrey took a breath. "One, two, three, four, five." The words came out in a row. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" She had counted all her peas.

Then her cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table. It made a little river. "Oh no," said Aubrey. Ben grabbed a towel. He wiped the river away. "The milk spilled because the cup tipped," said Aubrey. Ben smiled. "That's right. Let's move your cup away from your elbow."

Aubrey moved the cup. Then she ate one pea. "Nine left!" she said. "Nine, eight, seven." Ben laughed and clapped. Aubrey popped another pea in her mouth. "Six!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Charlie sat in her reading nook. She had her big letter book. Sunlight poured in the window onto the pages. Charlie pointed at a letter. "B," she said. Then she saw another letter. "B," she said again. But Mama shook her head. "That one is D," said Mama. Charlie frowned. The b and the d looked like twins to her. She felt worried. "Too many letters look the same," she said.

Mama sat down close beside her. "Look with your eyes," said Mama. Charlie looked hard at the b. The stick came first, then the bump. She looked at the d. The bump came first, then the stick. Charlie said "b" and made the b sound, buh. She said "d" and made the d sound, duh. "They are not the same!" she said. "The stick and the bump take turns!" She read the whole page with no mistakes. A feather from her pillow floated onto her lap. Charlie giggled. "My pillow is happy," she said. Mama gave her a kiss on her head. "My stinky little toes need a bath after this," Mama teased. Charlie laughed and hugged her book.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Ava went on a trip with Mom and Dad. Grandma came too. They drove a long way to the beach. "Why is the car ride so long?" Ava asked. "Because Grandma's house is far from the sand," Mom said. Ava looked out the window. She saw no sand, only trees.

At the beach, Ava wanted her yellow duck. It was not in her bag. "Why can't I get my duck?" she asked. "Because home is far away," Grandma said. "We can't drive back for one toy." Ava felt like crying a little. Grandma held her hand.

Then Grandma found a red ball. She put it in the water. The ball did not sink. It float-ed on top. "Look, it can float," Grandma said. Ava patted the water. The ball bobbed up and down. Ava laughed. Her trip was short on toys but big on fun. Grandma sat close by her on the warm sand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Ivy got a little blue card. It was her very own library card. Mom said, "You can pick one book." Ivy walked slowly along the shelves. She found a book about a worm in a garden. The worm had a dry leaf for a bed. "This one," said Ivy.

At the desk, the lady stamped the book. "Bring it back soon," she said. "Other kids want to read it too." Ivy held the book tight all the way home.

At home, Ivy read the worm book three times. She did not want to give it back. "I want to keep it forever," she said. But Mom said, "It has to go back, so other kids can read it too." So they took it back. Then Ivy saw a boy pick the worm book off the shelf. He sat down and opened it. He smiled. "He likes my worm book," said Ivy. Then she walked to the shelves to find a new one.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Raphael stood in the pool changing room. The floor was cool under his toes. The air smelled like soap and water. Dad was there, zipping up the swim bag.

"Look at my arm bands," said Raphael. One band was big and soft. One band was small and floppy. He pulled the floppy one on. It slid right down to his hand. Plop. It fell off on the wet floor. Raphael picked it up.

"Why did it fall off?" he asked. Dad smiled. "It has no air inside. We must blow it up." Dad blew and blew. The band grew fat and tight. Now it stayed on Raphael's arm. It would not slide at all.

"Water game time!" said Raphael. He held Dad's hand. They walked to the pool. The water was blue and shiny. Raphael splashed his feet at the edge. Dad held him close.

"You are safe with me," said Dad. Raphael kicked his legs. The tight bands made his arms float up high. He laughed out loud.

"Now I can swim," said Raphael. "Look at me go!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Sofia had a big red bag. She wanted to put her name on it. Her mom gave her sticker letters.

Sofia held up the letter S. "S says sss," she said. She put it on the bag. Then she held the letter O. "O says ah," she said. That went on next.

The letter F was tricky. Sofia looked at it. "Does F say buh?" she asked. She said buh, buh, buh. Then she said fff, fff, fff. Her lips bit her lip a little. "No, not buh," she said. "F says fff." She put the F on the bag.

She went slow. She stopped to look at each letter. One letter at a time.

At last the bag said SOFIA. Sofia smiled. "S, O, F, I, A," she read. Then she said each sound too. "Sss, ah, fff, ih, ah. Sofia!"

Mom clapped. Sofia hugged the big red bag.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Aaron stood in the pool changing room. His swim bag was open. He could not find his goggles. "Where did they go?" he asked. Dad looked in the big red bag. Then Dad looked in Aaron's shoe. There they were. Aaron put the goggles on. They felt tight, but good.

A lady had painted a huge house on the wall of the changing room. Aaron looked at it while Dad zipped up his suit. "Why do I need goggles?" Aaron asked. "Let's find out," said Dad. He held Aaron's hand and they walked to the pool.

First Aaron put his face in the water with no goggles. His eyes felt funny and he sat up fast. Then he put his face in with the goggles on. The water stayed out. He could see the blue tiles at the bottom. "I can see because the goggles keep the water away!" said Aaron. Dad smiled and held him close. "Now let's swim to the wall," said Dad. Aaron kicked his legs and off he went.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Liam woke up and ran to the window. He looked outside. The sun was out. "Sunny today!" he said. He put on his sun hat and went out to play.

Then the wind came. The wind blew his hat right off. The hat flew across the grass. Liam ran after it. "Why did my hat fly away?" he asked. He picked it up and held it tight. "The wind pushed it. Wind is strong." The wind made the tree leaves dance too.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip on Liam's nose. He ran inside fast. Mom gave him a raincoat and boots. Now he could jump in the puddles. After playing, he came in for warm juice. Mom dried his hair so it stood up straight. Liam laughed and took a big sip.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Sara took her orange cat toy to the playground. She wanted to play house. But she had no house!

First she found a big box. "This is my house," she said. Next she found a leaf. "This is my plate." Last she found a stick. "This is my spoon." One box, one leaf, one spoon. Now her house was ready.

Baby cat was hungry. Sara scooped sand with the spoon. She held it to the toy's soft mouth. "Eat, baby," she said. Then the wind blew. The leaf plate flew away! Sara looked around. Why did it fly? The wind did it, she thought. Wind makes light things fly.

She picked up the leaf and put a small stone on it. The wind blew again. This time the leaf stayed. "Heavy things stay put," said Sara. She patted baby cat. "Time for sleep." She drew a picture in the sand with her finger. It was a bed for baby cat. "Goodnight, house," Sara whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emilia went to the library with her dad. She found a book about a sleepy bear. She loved it. She hugged it. "I want to keep this book forever," she said.

Dad shook his head. "We take it home now. We bring it back another day." Emilia held the book tight. She did not want to let go. Her foot gave the floor a little kick. Thump. Thump.

Dad helped her count. "One week, then we bring it back," he said. Emilia counted too. "One week," she said.

At home, Emilia read the book. She opened the front first. The words told her what to say. She read it one time, two times, three times.

On the big day, Emilia held the book in both hands. She put it on the library desk. A boy picked it up next. "Now he can read it," Emilia said. She smiled and went to find a new book.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Amelia ran to the play kitchen at daycare. "I will make soup!" she said. She put a red pot on the stove. But the stove had no knobs today. Miss Kim had taken them off to wash.

Amelia peeked into the toy box. No knobs there either. How would her soup cook?

Then she saw Ben. Ben held a teddy bear. Ben wrapped the teddy in a small blanket. "The teddy is cold," said Ben. He patted the teddy's arm. "Sleep now."

Amelia had an idea. She did not need a knob. She could pretend! She turned her hand round and round in the air. "Click!" she said. "The stove is on now!"

Ben ran over. "Soup! My teddy is hungry." Amelia filled a bowl with pretend soup. Ben held it to the teddy's mouth.

"The teddy ate it all because I pretended the stove was on," said Amelia. "Now I will make tea!" She turned her hand in the air again. "Click!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Clara wants to build a big tower at school. She gets the big blocks first. Big blocks go on the bottom. Then she adds the small blocks on top. The tower grows tall, tall, tall.

Tom runs by fast. His feet go boom, boom, boom on the floor. The big tower wiggles. It falls down with a crash. Clara says, "Running fast made it fall." Tom says, "Sorry. That was naughty of me." He helps sweep up the blocks with his hands.

The teacher gives them warm milk and a cold apple. "Ouch, hot!" says Clara, and blows on her cup. She waits a bit. Now the milk is just right. Tom eats his cold apple. It goes crunch.

Tom walks slow, slow, slow back to the blocks. His feet go tip, tip, tip. Clara stacks the blocks again. Big on the bottom. Small on top. The tower stands tall and still. Clara laughs. "Slow feet keep my tower up!" Tom smiles and claps.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Alexander sat in the music room. A big drum sat in front of him. It had a picture of a pig on the side. His sweater was itchy, so he tugged the sleeve up.

Alexander hit the drum with his hand. Boooom. The sound was low and slow. He wanted a big, bouncy sound. He hit it again. Boooom. Still low.

Miss Rosa sat down next to him. "Try this," she said. She pulled the drum skin tight with her hand. "Now tap it."

Alexander tapped the tight skin. Bim! The sound was high and quick. He tapped again. Bim, bim, bim!

"The tight skin makes a fast sound," Alexander said. "The loose skin makes a slow sound."

"That's right," said Miss Rosa.

Alexander pulled the skin tight and played a fast song. Then he let go and played a slow song. Booom, bim, bim, booom. The pig on the drum looked like it was dancing.

"I did it," said Alexander. He patted the pig and played one more song.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story: Jake wanted to know his five senses. Mom said, "You can learn them right here." Jake looked at the sun in the backyard. It was too bright. "My eyes see the sun," Jake said. "My eyes are for seeing!" He ran to the rose bush. He sniffed a red rose. "My nose smells," Jake said. "My nose is for smelling!" A bee buzzed by. Jake heard the buzz. "My ears are for hearing," Jake said. Then a leaf fell on his head. He touched it with his hand. "My hand is for touching," Jake said. "But what is left?" Jake asked. Mom handed him a sweet strawberry. Jake took a bite. "Yum! My mouth is for tasting!" he said. Mom smiled. "You did it. All five!" Jake counted them on his fingers. He wiped strawberry juice off his chin. "That was nice," Jake said. "Can we do it again tomorrow?" Mom laughed. "Yes, we can."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Matthew went to the store with Dad. He wanted to make a fruit salad. He needed apples for it.

Dad held up a big red apple. "How many do we need?" he asked.

"Ten apples!" said Matthew. "One, two, three, four, five." He put apples in the bag one by one.

"Is that ten yet?" Matthew asked himself. He looked into the bag and counted again. "No. One, two, three, four, five. Only five." Five was not ten. He needed more apples.

So he kept going. He put in more apples, one at a time. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Now the bag was full.

"I counted more, so now I have more," said Matthew. "Five was too little. Ten is just right!"

At the checkout, a warm lamp glowed above the fruit. Matthew held the bag against his chest. "Ten apples," he said. "Can we make the salad now?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Aurora sat on the big clean couch. Everyone had come to watch the game. Uncle Max brought a bag of popcorn. Dad turned on the TV. But the screen stayed dark.

"TV needs the little box," said Aurora. She pointed at the remote. It was under the popcorn bag. Dad picked it up. He pushed the red button. The screen lit up. The game came on. Everyone clapped.

At half time, Mom went to stir the soup. Aurora smelled it from the couch. The pot was too big for the little stove burner, so Mom moved it to the big one. Then the soup began to bubble. "The big burner is hot enough," Aurora said. Uncle Max laughed and gave her a handful of popcorn. She ate it slowly and watched the players run.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Elijah found a bowl of sticky notes on the table. Each note had one big letter on it. There was an A and an M and a B.

Elijah wanted to write his mama's name. But he did not know which letters to pick. He picked the B first. He said its sound, "buh." Banana starts with B. Mama does not.

Then he picked the M. He said its sound, "mmm." The sound tickled his lips. Mama starts with "mmm!" He stuck the M on the wall.

Next he picked the A. He said, "ah." Apple starts with A. Mama starts with "ah" too. He stuck the A next to the M. Then he stuck up another M and another A, because he needed two of each.

Elijah pointed at the letters. "M, ah, M, ah," he said slowly. Then he said it fast. "Mama!"

Mama came to the wall. She gave him a soft hug. "My name!" she said.

"Yes," said Elijah. "The M makes my lips tickle. So I found it fast."

He stuck one more note on the wall. It was the letter E. "E is for Elijah," he said. "My turn now."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Ellie went to the library with Dad. She wanted a book about a bunny. She looked at the shelf. The books were all mixed up.

Ellie found a book about cars. "That is not a bunny," she said. She found a book about apples. "Apples are food. Bunnies are animals." She put it back. She found a book about teddy bears. "Bears are toys. Toy bears, toy trains, toy blocks. But I want an animal."

Ellie looked at the pictures on each book. Cars had wheels. Food was good to eat. Toys were for playing. Animals had fur and feet. Then she saw long ears on a cover. She opened the book. A bunny hopped in the pictures.

"The bunny is an animal, like a cat and a dog!" said Ellie. Dad smiled. "You found it. Books go in the right spot when we look."

Ellie sat on the big pillow by the window. She got sleepy as Dad read. One bunny, two bunnies, three baby bunnies in the book. Ellie closed her eyes just a little. "Read the hopping part again," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Ella sat on her bed with her library book. She wanted to keep it forever. It had a picture of a big cloudy sky on the front.

She looked at the front cover. It had little words on it. "Mom, what do the words say?" she asked. Mom said, "They say The Cloudy Day. Words on books tell you things." Ella turned the pages one by one, front to back. "Is this how we read?" she asked. "Yes, from the front to the back," said Mom.

Eella brushed her hand over the smooth page. She saw paint spots on the corner. "Oh no," she said. She wanted to fix them. She tried to rub the paint off. It stayed. She waited and looked again. Then Mom said, "Tomorrow the book goes back. Other kids get to read it too." Ella held the book close. "Can we get it again?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, we can borrow it again." Ella turned to the last page. "The end," she read out loud.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Maeva held a small clay lamp. It had one little flame. The flame was for Diwali, the festival of lights.

A big wind came. It blew the flame out. The lamp went dark. "Why did it go out?" asked Maeva. "The wind blew it," she said. Papa lit it again with a match.

Maeva walked slow. She cupped her hands around the flame. The wind could not reach it now. The flame stayed on. It did not go out.

People smiled at her lamp. Grandma gave her a sweet in a bowl. Maeva ate it with a spoon. The sweet was warm and soft.

Her shoe began to slip off. She stopped and pulled it back on. Papa waited for her. He held her hand so she would not fall.

At home they set the lamp by the door. "Why does it go there?" Maeva asked. "To light the way," said Papa. The little flame glowed and glowed. Maeva waved to it. "Good night, little light," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Luka sat on the park bench with his big sister, Mia. He wanted to win the game she played at school. "You name a sense and a body part," Mia said. "Then you get a gold star." Luka had no gold stars yet.

A dog ran by. "Woof, woof!" Luka put his hands over his ears. "My ears hear the dog!" Mia smiled and clapped. "Yes! Hearing uses your ears. One star for you."

Luka saw a tiny bug on a leaf. He pointed at it. "My eyes see the bug!" Mia clapped again. "Seeing uses your eyes. Two stars!"

Then Luka picked a red flower. He sniffed it with his nose. "My nose smells the flower! The rain made it smell good. That is why it smells so sweet." Mia laughed. "Three stars! Smelling uses your nose."

Next, Mia gave him a sweet berry. Luka began to chew. "Yum! My mouth tastes it!" Then he touched the wet slide. "My hands feel it! Hands are for touching!" Mia jumped up. "Five stars, Luka!"

Luka held up his hand and wiggled all five fingers. "Five senses, five stars!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Athena went to the park with her red ball. The ball was round and bouncy. She kicked it near a big tree. Then the ball rolled down the hill. It rolled right into the pond. Splash!

Athena stood at the water. "My ball!" she said. She could not reach it. Then she saw the ball sit on top of the water. "The ball floats," she said. It floated because it was light and full of air. A duck swam past. The duck pushed the ball with its beak. The ball came closer and closer.

Athena picked up a little stick. She held it out. The duck nudged the ball again. Athena grabbed her ball. "Thank you, duck," she said. She sat under the tree and ate a round apple. She dropped a piece of crust in the water. The duck ate it up. "Ducks like food, not toys," Athena said. The duck gave a happy quack.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Abigail sat at the little table. She wanted to draw on the tablet. She pressed the round button once. The screen stayed black. She pressed it again. Still black. She frowned.

Then she held the button down. She counted, "One, two, three." The screen lit up. It was bright and round like a moon. "It needed a long press," said Abigail. "A little tap does not work."

She found the drawing app and drew a tree. She drew one root, then two roots. She drew a bird ready to fly. "Time to put it away," said Teacher Jo.

Abigail pressed the button again. She held it down. The screen went dark. She set the tablet on the shelf, flat and safe.

"Look, Teacher Jo," she said. "I can do it all by myself."

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Penelope loved to color at daycare. She colored a big red cat. Then she colored her own hands red, too.

"Look, red hands!" said her friend Milo. He laughed. Red paint was on his nose, too.

The teacher rang the snack bell. Penelope reached for a cracker. The cracker turned red where her fingers touched it. "Oh no," she said. "My hands make the cracker red!"

The kind teacher took her to the little sink. Warm water ran over Penelope's hands. The soap made bubbles. She rubbed and rubbed. The red went down the drain. Her hands were clean now.

Penelope picked up a new cracker. It stayed plain and crunchy. "Wet hands get clean," she said. Then she ate it all up.

After snack came a nap. Penelope lay on her mat and hugged her red cat picture. "Sleep now," she whispered. She closed her eyes, and the room went quiet.

At the end of the day, Mommy helped her put on her coat. "One arm, then the other arm," said Mommy. Penelope pulled the zipper up all by herself. "I did it!" she said. Mommy kissed her red-cat picture.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Charlie stood at the gate of the school playground. Her tummy felt jumpy. She did not know anyone yet. A boy ran past her without saying hello.

Her teacher gave her a sticker for her shirt. It said Charlie in big red letters. "Now your name can talk for you," said the teacher. A girl came near the slide. She looked at the sticker. "Hi, Charlie," the girl said. "My name is Mia." The sticker told Mia her name! That is why the boy ran past. He could not read her mind, only her shirt.

Charlie and Mia dug in the sandbox together. They found a pink worm. It wiggled and made them laugh. "Silly worm," said Charlie. Their ice pops began to melt in the sun, so they sat in the shade. Charlie licked hers slowly. Mia waited for her too. "See you tomorrow," said Mia.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Felix sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. He hoped she would love it.

"I will paint her green frog," said Felix. But there was no green paint. Not one drop.

Felix looked and looked. He saw red paint. He saw yellow paint. He saw blue paint. No green. He felt a little scared. Then Miss Ada said, "Try mixing two colors."

Felix dipped his brush in yellow. He dipped his brush in blue. Swish, swish, swish. The paint turned green! It bubbled like a magic potion.

"Yellow and blue make green!" said Felix. He painted a big green frog. Then he mixed red and yellow. Swish, swish. That made orange, like a little sunset in his cup.

Yellow and blue make green. Yellow and blue make green. Felix said it two times, like a song.

At home, Felix gave Grandma the picture. "A green frog!" said Grandma. "And I made the green myself," said Felix. "Blue went in, yellow went in, and poof! Green came out."

Grandma kissed his head. Then they hung the frog on the fridge, right next to the orange sunset.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story: Ava sat in her car seat. Her tummy made a little growl. "I want a snack," she said. Mom handed her the snack bag from the front seat. Ava looked inside. She saw a red apple. She saw a cheese stick. Then she saw a banana. She picked up the banana. It felt hard and light. She peeled it a little. There was no fruit inside. It was yellow plastic all the way. It was her toy banana from the play kitchen! "Silly me," said Ava. "Toys are not food." She put it back in her bag. Then she took the apple. It was cold and sweet. She ate it slowly. "The apple is real food," she said. "It makes my tummy quiet." Mom smiled at the red light. The car went over a small bump. Ava held up the toy banana. "You sleep in my toy box," she told it. Then she looked out the window. A cow stood by a fence. "That is an animal," said Ava. "It eats real food too."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Gianna stood at the big airport window. A plane came in. Was Grandma on that one? Gianna had a question. She asked it out loud. "Is Grandma here now?"

Mom said, "Soon. Watch the door."

A man pulled a little bag. The bag rolled behind him. Why did it roll? Gianna looked down. The bag had wheels! Wheels make bags roll.

Then the door opened. Grandma! She pulled a big, big bag. It rolled too. Gianna laughed.

"Why is your bag so big?" she asked.

"I stay for a whole week," said Grandma. "Seven days. Seven sleeps."

Gianna counted on her fingers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Seven sleeps!

"That's a lot of clothes," said Gianna.

"It is," said Grandma. "And I packed my fishing pole. We will fish at the pond."

"Fish? Like the fish in my book?"

"Just like that. Real ones. We will catch one, and then we will let it go."

Gianna jumped up and down. She pulled the big bag a little bit. It rolled beside her.

The sky outside turned dark. The clouds looked big and mean. Would the plane go away?

"No rain yet," said Mom. "Run fast!"

They ran to the car. Seven sleeps, seven days. Gianna said it all the way home.

Grandma said, "And one fish."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Elizabeth stood by the cubbies at school. Her coat was on. But the zipper would not zip up. She pulled and pulled. Nothing happened.

Teacher Sam waited by the door. He did not rush her. Elizabeth sat down on the little bench. She looked at her zipper. She saw the two sides at the bottom. They were apart. She pushed one side down into the little slot. It made a small click. Then she pulled the zipper tab up. The zipper teeth came together, one by one. All the way to the top!

"Look! The zipper goes up when the bottom is in," Elizabeth said. Teacher Sam smiled. "Yes, it does," he said. Elizabeth laughed and ran to the puzzle table. She was fast. Her coat stayed warm and closed all morning.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Madelyn woke up with a big wish. She wished for her red apple in the blue bowl. She ran to the kitchen. "Apple, apple," she sang. But her hands were all sticky. Why were they sticky? She had eaten jam at breakfast. Jam on her hands made them sticky.

Mommy said, "Sticky hands need a bath." Madelyn looked at the water. She patted it with one finger. Bubbles went up, up, up. Mommy washed her hands and the sticky went away. "The water took the jam off," said Madelyn. "Because I washed!"

After the bath, Madelyn needed to get dressed. She picked her wild shirt with tigers on it. She pulled it on all by herself. Her hair was wet. Wet hair, dry shirt. She felt warm and clean.

Then came her apple, washed and shiny. She took a big bite. Crunch! Madelyn smiled and said, "I washed my hands, so now my apple is clean to eat." She ate it all up, down to the little brown seed.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Henri ran into Grandpa's house. "The baby is here!" he shouted. "My sister is here!" Grandpa smiled big. The baby lay in a soft blanket. Henri had a toy worm in his pocket. He wanted Baby May to hold it. He put the worm in her little hand. The worm slid right off. It fell on the floor. Henri tried again. It fell again. "She won't hold it," said Henri.

Grandpa did not say a word. He just tapped Henri's hand. Henri looked at his own finger. He put his finger in the baby's palm. May squeezed it! She held on tight! "She likes my finger!" Henri laughed. "Babies can hold fingers, not worms." Grandpa brought cold juice and frozen strawberries. They sat by the baby.

Then May made a funny face. She let go of Henri's finger. She grabbed Grandpa's big thumb instead. Henri followed it all the way to her cheek. "She chose you, Grandpa!" said Henri. Grandpa winked. "Now give her the worm," he said. Henri laid the worm on her tummy. May held her own hands on top of it. "She did it her own way!" said Henri.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Mateo sat at the little table in art class. He wanted to paint a house for his teacher's new baby. He poured some purple paint into his cup. The paint went plop, plop.

First he painted a big square. It had four sides, all the same. The square fell over in his mind. "A house needs a roof," said Mateo. A square roof would not fit. Then he saw it. He turned his brush and made a triangle. The triangle had three sides. It sat right on top of the square. "It fits!" said Mateo. The triangle roof worked because it was pointy on top and flat on the bottom.

Next he painted a purple door. It was a rectangle. It was tall like him. He made one window shaped like a circle. The circle was round like a ball. It rolled nowhere, it just stayed round.

His friend Lily looked over. "My roof fell off," she said. Mateo held up his brush. "Make a triangle," he said. "Three sides. Flat on the bottom." Lily tried it. Her triangle roof sat on top of her square. It did not fall. "It fits!" said Lily. Mateo gave her a big smile. He painted a tiny circle baby inside the house. The teacher clapped her hands. "Two houses," she said. "And one small baby." Mateo dipped his brush in purple one more time.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Harrison stood at the bus stop with Mama. The wind blew hard. It blew his hat right off his head. The hat flew up, up, up. "Oh no," said Harrison. "My hat went away!" He ran and got his sweet blue hat. He held it with both hands.

Then rain began to fall. Pit, pat, pit, pat. Big Mama opened her umbrella. Harrison stood under it too. The rain tapped on top. "Why do we need the umbrella?" he asked. "The rain is wet," said Mama. "It keeps us dry." The rain made little drops on the tip of his shoe. One drop sat on his toe through the hole in his sock.

The rain stopped. The sun came out. It was warm on his face. Harrison took off his mittens. "My hands are hot in the sun," he said. "The wind needs mittens. The sun does not." He put them in his pocket.

The bus came at last. Harrison climbed up one big step. "The wind blew my hat, so I hold it tight," he told the bus driver. The driver smiled. Harrison sat down by the window, hat on his lap.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Henri sat in the big salon chair. He held his doll, Pip. Today Henri would get his very first haircut. The chair felt tall. His feet did not touch the floor.

The hairdresser, Mia, put a soft cape on him. "Snip, snip," went her scissors. Henri shut his eyes tight. Then he opened one eye. Little bits of hair fell on the cape. They fell on his arm too. It did not hurt at all. Henri looked at Pip. "Hair has no hurt in it," he said. "That is why the scissors are okay."

Mia smiled. "That's right." A bit of hair fell on Pip's head. Henri laughed. "Pip looks silly with hair!" He brushed it off. Then a little pile spilled onto the floor, soft as snow.

Mia gave him a mirror. Henri saw his short hair. "I like it," he said. He hugged Pip tight.
